bipartite.note: The translator preserves the basic contrast between the fisher's sleeves whose color the sea 'ne'er thieves' and the speaker's own sleeves whose colors 'pass' (fade) due to tears; the juxtaposition is maintained but simplified into a clean antithesis (theirs unchanged / mine changed) rather than the more paradoxical layered structure of the original where the ama's sleeve wetness itself stands in for the speaker's weeping.

kakekotoba_handling.note: The physical wetness of the fisherman's sleeve is rendered ('oft-drenched sleeve'), but the doubled intensity (ぬれにぞぬれし) that also evokes the speaker's own tear-weeping is not carried by this phrase; the emotional/tearful reading is instead relocated to lines 5-6 ('tear-bedewed') as a separate, explicit statement rather than as a pivot fused into the same word.

kigo_handling.note: No seasonal marker exists in the source (kigo marked 'none') and none is introduced in the translation; the imagery of sea, sleeves, and tears remains in the timeless love/grief register rather than any seasonal one.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Dickens prioritizes a rhymed, metrical English quatrain-plus-couplet form over literal fidelity, expanding the wish and separating the pivot's double meaning into distinct explicit statements to make the implicit contrast fully overt for an English readership.

kakekotoba_handling.note: The translator renders the doubled verb as straightforward physical wetness ('wet through') applied to the fishers' sleeves, capturing the literal soaking but not linking it explicitly to the secondary meaning of weeping; the emotional weeping is instead relocated to a separate new line about the speaker's own 'tearful sleeves', so the pivot's simultaneous double-reference is split into two separate images rather than fused in one word.

kigo_handling.note: As per the source analysis this expression is not a seasonal kigo but a love-poem/utamakura image; the translation appropriately conveys no seasonal atmosphere, focusing instead on the tear-soaked sleeve motif and the utamakura place name 'Oshima island', consistent with the non-seasonal nature of the original.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi favors clarity and emotional directness, unpacking the poem's implicit tear/wetness pivot into an explicit final exclamatory line about the speaker's own sleeves, sacrificing the subtlety of the kakekotoba for immediate comprehensibility to an English readership.

bipartite.note: Porter keeps the contrastive logic — the fisher's clothes withstand the wetting while the speaker's own sleeve is discolored by tears — but compresses/simplifies it into an explicit 'but see I' contrast rather than the source's subtler paradox of 'even the ama's constantly-soaked sleeve does not change color, yet mine has.' The comparison is stated rather than implied, and the utamakura specificity (Ojima) is dropped, weakening the original's allusive juxtaposition into a more generic love-complaint parallel.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Porter renders the literal soaking of the fisher's clothes ('the drenching they receive') and separately supplies 'floods of tears' for the speaker's own weeping, but he splits the doubled pivot into two distinct images (fisher's wetness vs. speaker's tears) rather than having a single word carry both physical and emotional wetness simultaneously — so the kakekotoba's fused double meaning is not preserved in one term, only the primary literal sense is attached to 'drenching' while the secondary sense is explained separately via 'floods of tears.'

kigo_handling.note: No seasonal word or atmosphere is present; Porter converts the utamakura 'Ojima no ama' into a generic 'fisher's clothes, though cheap' image, losing both the place-name allusion and any seasonal resonance the source analysis notes is largely absent anyway.

Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes producing a smooth, rhymed English love-lyric that states the emotional contrast explicitly, sacrificing the utamakura place-name, the fused kakekotoba wordplay, and subtlety of implication in favor of clarity and metrical closure.

kakekotoba_handling.note: McCauley renders the doubled verb literally as physical soaking of the fisherwomen's sleeves, capturing the primary meaning vividly with repetition ('wet through and wet again'), but there is no signal of the secondary meaning of the speaker's own tears/weeping — the word 'wet' stays purely literal with no emotional undertone supplied.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley prioritizes a literal, line-by-line rendering of the imagery and syntax, preserving the surface meaning of the ama's soaked-but-colorfast sleeves while leaving the poem's implicit emotional comparison to the reader's inference.
